articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ϵ). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

articles.title: A New Degree of Freedom in Stellarator Coil Design
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reversed toroidal field (RTF) coils introduce a new degree of freedom in stellarator coil design. While the total plasma-linked current is fixed by Ampere's law, compensating RTF currents allow the modular-coil current to exceed this value without altering the net linkage. This redistribution decouples key coil constraints and modifies the external coil geometry without significantly compromising the confining magnetic field. As a result, the achievable coil-plasma separation can be increased in the configurations studied, potentially enabling more compact stellarator designs.

articles.title: Latent Diffusion Modeling of Two- and Three-dimensional Fracture Networks with Sparse Observation Conditioning
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Characterizing subsurface fracture networks is challenging because geometry and connectivity are sparsely observed and uncertain away from measurements. We develop a latent diffusion framework for unconditional and observation-conditioned generation of two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) fracture networks. Fractures and the surrounding matrix are represented as binary fields and compressed by a variational autoencoder into compact spatial latent representations, where an Elucidated Diffusion Model learns their distribution. The 3D model operates on native volumetric fields, with a reconstruction objective designed to preserve sparse, thin fracture structures. Sparse borehole observations are incorporated through a conditioning encoder, classifier-free guidance, and diffusion posterior sampling. Generated ensembles reproduce key fracture-network statistics, including fracture area/volume fraction, two-point correlation, and chord-length distributions. Reconstructed fracture counts and gas-production responses are comparable to those of the reference networks under the considered multiphase flow scenarios. Conditional generation satisfies 99.6% of prescribed well observations in 2D. In 3D, where vertical boreholes constrain full voxel columns, conditional realizations satisfy 84.2% of observed well voxels while maintaining fracture volume and geometry comparable to the reference ensemble. These results demonstrate the potential of latent diffusion models as compact probabilistic representations for fracture-network characterization, ensemble generation, and sparse-observation conditioning.
authors: Jiawei Shen, Hongkyu Yoon, Jonghyun Lee

articles.title: Learning Electron Density with Virtual Atoms for Transferable Atomistic Representations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electron density is a fundamental quantity of electronic structure, yet most machine learning density models treat it solely as a reconstruction target and are developed separately from machine learning interatomic potentials. Here, we introduce a virtual-atom formulation within the DPA3 framework, in which density query points are represented as virtual nodes and processed by the same parameterized encoder used for real atoms. An asymmetric neighbor construction allows virtual atoms to receive information from nearby real atoms without altering the real-atom interaction graph. The resulting framework supports density, energy, and force prediction through task-specific readout heads. The proposed model achieves state-of-the-art density reconstruction accuracy on the Materials Project benchmark, matches the best reported performance on nickel-manganese-cobalt battery cathode materials, and is competitive with dedicated density models on QM9. When density labels are used jointly with energy and force supervision, the model improves in-domain accuracy, makes local environment information more accessible under linear probing, and reduces zero-shot force errors on larger QM40 molecules. Density-only checkpoints also provide useful initializations for downstream energy-force learning under the fixed fine-tuning protocol. Together, these results support electron density as a source of electronic-structure supervision for interatomic-potential representations.
authors: Yuzhi Liu, Xinzijian Liu, Chengqian Zhang, Anyang Peng, Duo Zhang, Han Wang

articles.title: Learn the Dynamics, Enforce the Physics: Generative Latent Operators for High-Dimensional Beam Evolution
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation is indispensable for modeling beam dynamics in particle accelerators, but its computational cost limits many-query workflows, such as configuration exploration, virtual diagnostics, and controller design. We introduce GLOBE, a physics-constrained Generative Latent Operator for Beam Evolution, modeling the nonlinear, control-dependent, multiscale evolution of 3D beam--field dynamics covering 10⁷ spatial cells. GLOBE compresses beam--field states into a compact latent space and factors their evolution into two components. A control-conditioned neural operator learns the dominant dynamics, while an amplitude-normalized generative model captures the residual distribution, recovering fine-scale structures and conditional variations. GLOBE enforces field constraints by regime-specific, parameter-free operators: a Poisson solve reconstructs the electric field in the electrostatic regime, and a spectral projection imposes Gauss's law and a divergence-free magnetic field in the electromagnetic regime. On two high-resolution 3D particle-accelerator benchmarks, bunched-beam transport and plasma-wakefield acceleration, GLOBE lowers relative-L₂ error by 9% and 13%, low-frequency spectral error by 69% and 51%, and mid-frequency spectral error by 54% and 20% relative to the strongest baseline (DPOT), satisfies field constraints, and reduces hours of PIC simulation to a minute per rollout.
authors: Haohan Zou, Alexander Scheinker, Yuanyuan Shi

articles.title: Maximal Axion Optical Chirality Enabled by Degenerate Quasibound States in the Continuum
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Axion quasiparticles introduce magnetoelectric coupling in topological materials, yet their optical signatures are intrinsically weak, severely limiting experimental detection and practical exploitation. Here, we demonstrate maximal optical chirality of axion quasiparticles by coupling them with degenerate quasibound states in the continuum (qBICs). By integrating three-dimensional topological insulators (3DTIs) with achiral photonic crystal slabs (PCSs), we reveal that axion quasiparticles induce an effective Zeeman effect that lifts the degeneracy of achiral qBICs in PCSs, splitting them into two nondegenerate high-Q chiral qBICs with maximally opposite chirality. These result in a more than 10³⁻ and 200-fold increase in the polarization conversion efficiency and Faraday rotation angle, respectively, compared to the intrinsic chiroptical response of bare 3DTI films. Moreover, circular dichroism and nonreciprocal optical responses are revealed as new key signatures for probing axion quasiparticles in 3DTI-PCS coupled systems. Our results provide a definitive route for observing axion quasiparticles and topological physics, while establishing a promising platform for controlling optical polarization, spin, phase, and nonreciprocal responses.
authors: Chang-Yin Ji, Chong Wang, Jiafang Li, Yugui Yao

articles.title: Learning native eddy-resolving ocean dynamics outperforms coarse emulation and downscaling
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Eddy-resolving ocean simulations are essential for representing mesoscale dynamics that regulate ocean circulation, energy transport, and climate variability. However, they are costly to generate, store, and share. Artificial intelligence (AI) may help, but it remains unclear whether high-resolution ocean fields can be faithfully represented by evolving ocean states at coarse resolution followed by spatial downscaling, or whether dynamical evolution needs to be learned directly from native high-resolution simulations. We show that directly learning dynamical evolution on a 0.1ⁱ̧rc grid provides a more faithful representation of mesoscale variability than evolving ocean states on a 1ⁱ̧rc grid followed by downscaling reconstruction. We developed a full-depth 1ⁱ̧rc emulator and a native 0.1ⁱ̧rc sea surface temperature (SST) emulator, both of which remained stable over long-term free-running simulations without significant drift, providing reliable baselines for this comparison. Direct learning at 0.1ⁱ̧rc preserves mesoscale energy, spectral characteristics, and frontal gradients, whereas the coarse-resolution evolution followed by downscaling approach recovers large-scale patterns but fails to reproduce key mesoscale signatures. We show that the learned mesoscale statistics remain consistent across diverse hardware platforms, supporting the reproducibility and portability of AI-based ocean simulations. These results suggest that downscaling of low-resolution large-scale states alone is insufficient to represent ocean mesoscale variability, supporting the need to learn dynamical evolution directly in a high-resolution state space. These findings highlight the continued importance of high-resolution physics ocean models as a foundation for AI-based ocean simulation, providing dynamically resolved training data for physically faithful high-resolution emulators.
authors: Zilu Liu, Tao Zhang, Hailong Liu, Kai Xu, Qinghui Lin, Maoxue Yu, Jiangfeng Yu, Jingwei Xie, Zhao Jing, Minghua Zhang, Lixin Wu

articles.title: SPIRE: Spin-Resolved Particle-in-Cell with Radiative Corrections for Extreme Laser--Plasma Interactions
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present SPIRE, a spin- and photon-polarization-resolved particle-in-cell (PIC) code for self-consistent simulations of laser-plasma interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime. The classical PIC framework combines a Yee-grid finite-difference time-domain Maxwell solver, a relativistic Boris particle pusher, shape-function particle-grid interpolation, Esirkepov charge-conserving current deposition, laser boundary injection, and a relativistic moving window in one, two, and three spatial dimensions. A vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian laser injector based on an angular-spectrum formulation supports tightly focused, nonparaxial optical orbital-angular-momentum modes. The strong-field QED module treats nonlinear Compton scattering and nonlinear Breit-Wheeler pair production as stochastic processes using spin- and polarization-resolved probabilities in the local constant-field approximation. Electron and positron spin evolution includes stochastic transitions, no-emission corrections, and Thomas-Bargmann-Michel-Telegdi precession with a field-dependent anomalous magnetic moment. Photon polarization is represented by the Stokes vector and evolves through nonlinear Compton scattering, pair production, vacuum birefringence, and vacuum dichroism. The implementation is verified with one-, two-, and three-dimensional benchmarks. Classical PIC results are cross-checked against SMILEI, and the spin- and polarization-resolved QED modules reproduce published results for polarized electron generation, vacuum birefringence and dichroism, and dense polarized positron production. These benchmarks verify the coupled classical PIC, strong-field QED, spin, and photon-polarization modules implemented in SPIRE.
authors: Xian-Zhang Wu, Huai-Hang Song, Wei-Min Wang, Yan-Fei Li

articles.title: Plasma-neutral collision operators for hydrogen isotopes: kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions, comparison to fluid
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plasma-neutral interactions critically affect the edge dynamics of magnetically confined fusion devices. Neutral atoms modify ion and electron velocity distributions, potentially affecting local instabilities Standard fluid models simplify these processes (namely charge exchange, ionization and recombination) using Maxwellian assumptions and linearized source terms. We revisit these assumptions for a hydrogen plasma interacting with hydrogen atoms. We derive plasma-neutral interaction terms in the kinetic and gyrokinetic frameworks. Accounting for velocity-dependent differential cross-sections, the model captures the kinetic impact of inelastic collisions on ions and electrons beyond energy and momentum exchange. We demonstrate that the fluid moments of the kinetic model reduce to standard fluid source terms under the appropriate assumptions of Maxwellianity and linearity. We compare the kinetic model with fluid models through their effects on distribution functions and fluid moments. Substantial discrepancies are observed, even for Maxwellian distributions. For charge exchange, the kinetic model yields momentum and energy exchange rates up to twice those predicted by fluid descriptions. We show that a fluid treatment of ionization greatly overestimates the mean kinetic energy of the produced electrons. These results highlight the limitations of fluid descriptions and the importance of kinetic effects in edge-plasma momentum and energy exchange.
authors: Matthieu Protais, Guilhem Dif-Pradalier, Yanick Sarazin, Virginie Grandgirard, Yannick Marandet, Srikanth Sureshkumar, Naren Varadarajan

articles.title: Resonant dispersive wave emission: a route toward few-cycle, tunable strong-field drivers in the visible
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intense ultrafast lasers are the backbone of strong-field physics and enable table-top scale applications of coherent high-photon energy radiation through high-harmonic generation (HHG). Using short-wavelength drivers in HHG promises highly efficient conversion into the extreme ultraviolet, but short pulse durations are essential to this approach. We generate multi-GW peak power, sub-10 fs pulses in the visible with broad spectral tunability (220--752 nm) by harnessing soliton dynamics in large-core, gas-filled capillary fibers for high-energy resonant dispersive wave emission. This establishes the potential of resonant dispersive waves as a new class of driving lasers for HHG and strong-field physics in addition to widespread applications in ultrafast spectroscopy.
authors: Martin Gebhardt, Joleik Nordmann, Nikoleta Kotsina, Michael Heynck, Teodora Grigorova, Christian Brahms, John C. Travers

articles.title: Comparative Robustness of Mach-Zehender and Microring Photonic Matrix Multipliers Under Laser RIN and Thermal Drift
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic matrix multipliers can accelerate neural-network inference, but their practical utility depends on how optical weight elements respond to source noise, thermal variation, and calibration error. This paper compares Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM) and microring-resonator (MRR) implementations under laser relative-intensity noise (RIN), column-wise thermal/phase drift, and their joint action. Two CIFAR-10 classifiers - a compact four-layer CNN and ResNet-8 - are mapped to matched photonic multiply-accumulate chains using common source-distribution, detection, numerical, and calibration assumptions. Both architectures reproduce the same zero-perturbation baseline for each workload: 79.5% classification accuracy for the Small CNN and 70.0% for ResNet-8. Robustness is then evaluated using separate RIN-only and drift-only sweeps and a full two-dimensional RIN-drift grid, with dimensionless RMS perturbation levels extending from 0.5% to 20%. The analysis reports classification accuracy, class normalized confusion matrices, rolling-accuracy traces, one-dimensional robustness curves, and multidimensional response surfaces. Device equations and parameter definitions follow the models implemented in the QPI Labs Photonic Inference Simulator, with shared laser fluctuations propagated as correlated multiplicative noise and slow drift represented as a per-output-column perturbation of calibrated weights. All numerical results are generated from recorded experiment configurations and random seeds. The study provides a controlled system-level framework for comparing interferometric and resonant photonic weight elements while limiting conclusions to the implemented device models, perturbation ranges, calibration policy, and neural-network workloads.

articles.title: A reduced model for neoclassical transport in non-axisymmetric magnetic configurations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A unified framework is proposed to compute a neoclassical equilibrium for tokamaks with non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations, based on a Hamiltonian description combined with a variational approach that relies on a principle of minimum entropy production. This approach allows for a transparent identification of the respective contributions from different classes of trapped particles in magnetic well minima. Analytic expressions are derived for specific collisionality regimes, and a fast and efficient numerical procedure is devised to compute the entropy production rate. Finding the extremum of the entropy production leads to tractable expressions of transport coefficients that can be computed quickly and efficiently.
authors: Y. Ban, X. Garbet, R. Varennes, Z. Qu, K. Lim, Y. Sarazin, A. Ibrahim, Y. C. Tay, B. B. Ang

articles.title: Kernel-Level Constant-Potential Molecular Dynamics in GROMACS
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How charge rearranges within an electrode shapes the behavior of batteries, supercapacitors, and other electrochemical devices. Molecular simulations can capture this response by allowing the charge on each electrode atom to adjust to its surroundings, but repeatedly calculating these charges adds substantial computational cost. We present an open-source implementation of the constant-potential method in GROMACS that integrates these calculations into the program's optimized CPU and GPU routines. Comparisons with established codes validate the electrode charges, while charging, voltammetry, and impedance simulations demonstrate the response to changing electrical conditions. The implementation also supports electrodes that move or deform and models of finite metallic screening and electron spillover. In a pair of charged carbon nanotubes, allowing charge to move away from the facing surfaces reduces the repulsive force at contact by about half at an intermediate charge and keeps the pair bound where a uniform-charge model opens within the simulated time. These capabilities make the electrical response of electrodes accessible within GROMACS for studies of interfacial structure, charging dynamics, and electrode motion.
authors: Sheng Bi, Mathieu Salanne, Jun Cheng, Guang Feng

articles.title: Transfer learning-aided, artificial intelligence approach to evaluate optical properties of materials for classical and quantum photonic applications
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.15904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, an artificial intelligence-assisted evaluation of the refractive indices of different materials is performed. The evaluation of the refractive index is necessary to design photonic devices for various classical and quantum photonic applications, and to theoretically analyse experimental results. The refractive index is one of the crucial parameters that affect the interaction of light with matter. Although the refractive index can be measured experimentally, its estimation via computational means provide the advantage of not requiring costly instrumentation, trained researchers and could avoid potential laboratory-based uncertainties. Therefore, in this study, artificial intelligence is implemented to estimate the optical constants of two types of materials, i.e., noble metals, and semiconductors. To this end, an artificial neural network is used to estimate the real and the imaginary parts of the refractive index of a specific material for various wavelengths of light. Then, the knowledge of the trained neural network is employed to initiate and train new neural networks to estimate the refractive indices of other materials. For the training of a neural network, various methods can be deployed. However, the application of the training can be a time-consuming process. A transfer learning approach is here implemented to provide a faster training solution for the problem under study. The implementation of transfer learning allows training the neural networks for a new material with higher speed or accuracy when compared to non-knowledge transfer-based training. Our results show the efficiency of the proposed technique in accurately evaluating the real and imaginary parts of the refractive index of different materials.
authors: Mohammad Reza Habibi, Luca Sapienza, Juan C. Vasquez

articles.title: Implicit PIC Simulations of Hydrogen Plasmas with Intense Negative Ion Production
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-density plasma discharges in hydrogen operating at low pressures are of considerable interest for negative ion production used in many applications. Their weak collisionality requires a kinetic, nonlocal description, and a popular approach is to model such discharges numerically using the particle-in-cell (PIC) method combined with Monte Carlo collisions (MCC). However, the most commonly used explicit momentumconserving variant of this method is highly inefficient because it must resolve both the Debye length and the plasma period. In this context, the implicit energy-conserving PIC/MCC scheme appears to be an attractive alternative, as it can model the plasmas of interest using their actual parameters without resorting to artificial scaling techniques. This work considers simulations of two types of high-density plasma discharges performed using electromagnetic or electrostatic energy-conserving PIC/MCC codes in hydrogen, and discusses the observed negative ion production.

articles.title: Relativistic Six-Fluid Rotating-Plasma Force-Balance Equilibria for p-11B Fusion Conditions in Spherical Tori
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate an axisymmetric spherical torus (ST) six-component magnetofluid equilibrium model for p₁₁B plasmas composed of thermal and suprathermal proton, boron, and electron fluids. The model is designed for p₁₁B parameter regimes where ion energies, strong current drive, energetic electron populations, and ion-electron temperature separation can render a single_fluid staticₑquilibrium description inadequate. It generalizes rotatingₚₗₐₛₘₐ equilibrium theory by incorporating relativistic thermal enthalpy corrections to the electron fluids via h(T/mₑc²⁾ and by constructing modified flux functions Yα associated with canonical angular momentum for each component α. The equilibrium is determined by a Grad-Shafranov-like Ampere law for the poloidal magnetic flux Psi, algebraic density relations constrained by quasineutrality, and prescribed profile functions Fα(Yα), Tα(Yα) and Kα(Yα). The manuscript includes the relativistic magnetofluid equations, the axisymmetric equilibrium formulation, the six_fluid computational method, and four numerical equilibria: two reactorᵣₑₗₑᵥₐₙₜ ST p₁₁B parameter sets and two EHL-2 ST cases. The examples span toroidal beta b_T = 0.058₀.253, plasma currents Iₚ = 2.697₁₂.59 MA, and suprathermal electron temperatures Tₑₕ = 287 keV₂.37 MeV, with h up to 19.1. Over these parameter ranges, Ampere's law accuracy, electrostatic potential accuracy, and componentᵣₑₛₒₗᵥₑd radial force balance can have errors ranging from 3% to below 0.1%. These results indicate that high-temperature p₁₁B ST equilibria can differ qualitatively from the single_fluid tokamak equilibria and require analysis of equilibrium componentᵣₑₛₒₗᵥₑd force balance, relativistic electron enthalpy, and explicit reproducibility diagnostics.

articles.title: High Sensitivity Transient Holographic Full-Polarization Microscopy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The polarization state of light provides direct access to ultrafast electronic, magnetic, and structural dynamics in materials. Transient wide-field microscopy with simultaneous amplitude, phase, and polarization sensitivity enables spatially resolved measurements of these dynamics, but its sensitivity is often limited by technical noise and background fluctuations. Here, we demonstrate transient holographic full-polarization microscopy with substantially reduced instrumental noise and sensitivity approaching the shot-noise limit. We compare holographic geometries using one, two, and four reference beams and find that the single-reference configuration provides the most favourable shot-noise-limited sensitivity for the derived polarization observables. Combined with two-camera detection, it simultaneously captures both orthogonal polarization components without distributing reference photons among multiple carriers. A self-referenced noise-reduction framework combining singular value decomposition and background subtraction further suppresses correlated noise. For spatially averaged regions, the baseline noise is reduced by factors of three-sixty, enabling detection of weaker transient responses at lower excitation densities and in weakly absorbing materials.
authors: Julia A. Gessner, Philipp Kollenz, Godwin Maliyekkal, Milena R. Neubert, Garrett May, Lukas Becker, Nasrin Solhtalab, Tiago Buckup, Felix Deschler

articles.title: Kinematic saturation of the electromagnetically-induced-transparency peak in thermal atomic vapors
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate that, in thermal atomic vapors, the electromagnetically-induced-transparency (EIT) transmission peak exhibits saturation. Investigating the amplitude of the velocity-selected double-resonance transmission peak-a purely kinematic effect arising from finite wavevector mismatch-we identify a threshold atomic column density Ns. For column densities N below Ns, the amplitude of the transmission peak maximum increases with column density. Once it exceeds Ns, the peak amplitude maximum remains constant, while the corresponding detuning shifts away from resonance and scales as the square root of ln(N over Ns). Furthermore, We find that the operating point for optimum photon-shot-noise-limited sensitivity deviates from that of the transmission peak maximum. Our study provides guidance for optimizing EIT readout in vapor cell and for precision measurements built upon this scheme.
authors: Sheng-Xian Xiao, Jing-Yi Mao, Tao Wang

articles.title: Onset condition of the ramified-jet regime: an experimental and theoretical study
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16585v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study experimentally and theoretically investigates the electrically induced transition of a gas-focused liquid jet into a rim-emitting sheet. Ultra-high-speed imaging was used to examine the effects of applied voltage, gas and liquid flow rates, and liquid properties on sheet formation and breakup. Fully developed, quasi-stable sheets formed with ethanol, whereas isopropanol exhibited only initial sheet formation. Increasing voltage promoted sheet stretching, finer and more numerous rim jets, and a narrower spray. Higher gas flow rates shifted the transition towards the nozzle and produced finer structures, while higher liquid flow rates generated larger sheets with thicker rims. A first-order theoretical model assumes an equipotential interface and neglects finite charge relaxation, hydrodynamic perturbations, and nonlinear evolution. It balances destabilizing Maxwell-pressure perturbations against restoring capillary-pressure perturbations on a conducting cylindrical jet. The model identifies the elliptic azimuthal mode, m = 2, as the first unstable mode leading to sheet formation and predicts a critical electric Bond number of 3. Predicted onset voltages agree with measurements within 20%, and the threshold was consistent with published ramified-electrospray observations. The agreement with experiments supports electrocapillary symmetry breaking as the mechanism of onset and provides a compact, physically grounded criterion for predicting the transition from electrified jets to rim-emitting sheets.
authors: Bor Zupan, Jernej Kušar, Božidar Šarler

articles.title: QUARZ: a quasi-static particle-in-cell code with non-uniform radial grids for plasma wakefields
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a quasi-static particle-in-cell scheme for beam-driven plasma wakefields in cylindrical geometry that works on an arbitrary non-uniform radial grid. The field equations are discretized with hat-function finite elements and conservative finite volumes on any monotone set of radial nodes, and the transverse magnetic field is obtained explicitly, without iterations, following Baxevanis and Stupakov. An optional azimuthal mode m=1 describes beam offsets, tilts and hosing. The discretization keeps the discrete Gauss law exact, deposits a uniform plasma exactly on every node including the axis, and remains second-order accurate on smoothly stretched grids. Resolution can therefore be placed where the physics needs it. For a tightly focused witness beam that pulls the plasma ions onto the axis, a grid that is fine only near the axis gives the same near-axis fields as a uniform grid with the same axis resolution, with thirty times fewer cells and in thirty times less computing time. Such a grid also resolves the singular closure of a cold-plasma bubble, which a uniform grid hides by smoothing it over one cell; smoothing the plasma sources over a fixed length, chosen independently of the grid, regularizes the closure and makes the wake behind it converge. The scheme is implemented in the open-source C++/Kokkos code QUARZ (Quasistatic Arbitrary-resolution RZ), which runs on CPUs and GPUs and uses MPI with a pipelined decomposition along the co-moving coordinate. Simulations of the self-modulation of the AWAKE proton bunch agree with the three-dimensional code HiPACE++. QUARZ is, to our knowledge, the first production-grade simulation code in plasma physics that is emphzero-touch: all of its source code, tests and documentation were written by an AI agent directed by a physicist who did not write a single line of the code.

articles.title: Wireless Energy Transfer for Space Applications: A Review of Technologies, Mission Architectures, Energy Routing, and System Integration
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wireless energy transfer (WET) decouples energy generation from energy use, offering strategic advantages for distributed spacecraft, lunar surface networks, mobile assets, and high-power remote loads. This review organizes the field along four axes: physical mechanism, energy reference plane, mission architecture, and evidence maturity. It examines near field inductive and resonant transfer, microwave and millimeter wave power beaming, optical and laser-based transfer, space-based solar power, lunar and cislunar energy delivery, inter-spacecraft power sharing, intraspacecraft contactless interfaces, and reconfigurable or relay assisted routing within a common R0,R7 energy-accounting framework. Three conclusions emerge. First, WET is most valuable when spatial or temporal mismatches separate energy generation from load demand; it does not universally replace local generation or onboard storage. Second, dominant losses vary across system architectures. Beam collection, rectification, receiver output, and useful load efficiencies are therefore not directly comparable without explicitly defined energy reference planes. Third, technological maturity is uneven. High power ground demonstrations and short range flight applications are relatively well established, whereas long-range radiative inter spacecraft transfer, spaceborne routing hardware, lunar energy networks, and deep space applications remain supported primarily by models, simulations, and mission studies rather than hardware demonstrations. Progress requires validated end to end energy budgets under mission realistic constraints, including pointing and tracking, thermal management, environmental exposure, reliability, energy storage, and regulatory compliance.
authors: Lyuye Lin, Zhifu Feng, Ermanno Miele, Quanbo Ge, Manuel Iori, Chunbo Liu, Kwok-Tong Chau, Denis Garoli, Remo Proietti Zaccaria

articles.title: The point is a trap: Mathematics of Elastic States in Complex Multiscale Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.16994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Observables in complex biological systems are often reduced in their inherent complexity, resulting in abstract, a priori mathematical representations based on simple concepts such as points in spaces or interconnected nodes in lattices or networks. This reduction is relevant not only for the formulation of multiscale mathematical models and field theories but also for experimental planning and data collection to gain systematic evidence for the nature of such systems, thus extracting robust causal relationships that would lead to better control of the system. However, mathematical abstraction remains challenging and problematic, especially given the tightly intertwined elements between objects and their environment, the system's affordance, and the fact that all these aspects limit fundamental mathematical concepts such as set theory, thus hindering the definition of phase spaces in extreme cases. In this work, I introduce a potential axiomatic representing a nonreducible representation of high order structures representing entanglement between observables in complex systems and their environment, considering not only their coupling but also their affordance in relation to the overall system and context, and thus intend to formalize concepts already used in complex systems such as Kantian wholes. In light of this axiomatic, I identify states that are rather less elastic with respect to their environment, discuss how low elasticity enables the application of set theory, while high elasticity limits the mathematical representation of complex systems, and present an exemplary Ising model with a network of elastic states with respect to different contexts as a limiting case for mathematical modelling in this context.

articles.title: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to sim1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.
authors: Niko R. Reed, Declan M. Daly, Andrew J. Beling, Jordan D. Giandrea, Ronald L. Walsworth, John W. Blanchard, Daniel Ang

articles.title: Solvating machine-learning interatomic potentials for solution-phase chemistry
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are trained on gas-phase data, which limits their use for chemistry in solution. Here, we introduce AnySolv, a transferable implicit solvation potential that provides solvent-dependent energy and force corrections to existing gas-phase potentials without retraining them. It is trained on 1.4 million solvation energies and forces computed with density functional theory (DFT) and SMD in 36 solvents, spanning charged, open-shell, and transition-state structures. Because solvents are represented by continuous physical descriptors, AnySolv supports 179 solvents, including those absent from training. On external benchmarks, AnySolv reproduces DFT-SMD solvation energies to 2-4 meV mean absolute error at more than three orders of magnitude lower cost, and it matches the accuracy of DFT-SMD against experimental solvation free energies. This enables screening of the mechanisms of 120 nucleophilic aromatic substitution reactions in six phases as well as molecular dynamics simulations that reproduce the experimentally observed solvent-dependent conformational preferences of alanine dipeptide. By providing transferable solvation corrections to existing MLIPs, AnySolv enables scalable simulations of solvent-dependent chemical reactivity and molecular dynamics.

articles.title: Observation of Photon Bunching in Broadband Multimode Thermal Light Enabled by Temporal Imaging
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photons emitted by incoherent sources exhibit temporal bunching, a fundamental manifestation of Bose-Einstein statistics first observed by Hanbury Brown and Twiss (HBT). While intensity correlation measurements originated in astronomy and are now central across quantum technologies, biophysics, and spectroscopy, observing temporal bunching in broadband thermal light remains limited by detector temporal resolution. Conventional approaches - such as streak cameras or optical upconversion - introduce severe trade-offs in efficiency, bandwidth, or setup versatility. Here, we propose and demonstrate a third route: pre-detection temporal magnification of the optical field prior to measuring its intensity autocorrelation function in a conventional HBT setup. Using an electro-optic time lens with a temporal magnification of 660, we resolve the temporal intensity autocorrelation of broadband thermal light generated via non-degenerate spontaneous parametric down-conversion with a bandwidth of 250 GHz. This enables direct observation of thermal photon bunching on sub-3.5 picosecond timescales without narrow spectral filtering, establishing pre-detection temporal imaging as a general platform for broadband statistical optics, with applications spanning ultrafast quantum optics, biophysical imaging, and potentially stellar intensity interferometry.
authors: Filip Sośnicki, Michał Mikołajczyk, Sanjay Kapoor, Dmitri B. Horoshko, Mikhail I. Kolobov, Michał Karpiński

articles.title: HOM Mitigation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Higher Order Modes (HOMs) in accelerating structures are resonant electromagnetic fields excited and left behind by charged particle bunches. They can severely degrade the beam quality in accelerators, such as the multi-bunch energy spread and transverse emittance, and therefore one must carefully study and mitigate them. In this lecture, various methods of HOM mitigation are reviewed. On one hand, one tries to avoid their existence, for example by careful design of the accelerating structures and damping systems. On the other hand, one can reduce the effect of the excited HOM fields, for example by means of fast feedbacks or beam alignment. Additionally, a few ways to make HOM signals useful are referred to, such as diagnostics of the beam or of accelerating structures.

articles.title: Wisevolve Potential Engine: Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics at 100 Million Atom-Steps per Second on a Single GPU
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose molecular dynamics software supports diverse interatomic potentials and simulation requirements. Within a simulation stage, the loaded potential model and the required calculations typically remain fixed as the atomic configuration evolves. We present the Wisevolve Potential Engine (WPE), which uses this information from GPUMD to select and reuse a GPU execution policy tailored to the model and simulation stage. GPUMD retains simulation control and ownership of the simulation data. On a single NVIDIA RTX 5090, WPE-enabled GPUMD (GPUMD-WPE) achieves a median throughput of 109 million atom-step/s across 106 neuroevolution potential (NEP) workloads. For a 15.1-million-atom diamond Si system, it sustains 142 million atom-step/s. Relative to GPUMD, geometric-mean speedups are 3.49x across these NEP workloads, 3.61x across 16 workloads using NEP with dynamic charges (qNEP), 1.24x across 28 classical-potential workloads, and 10.5x across 56 path-integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) configurations. End-to-end calculations of water structure, lattice thermal conductivity, and PIMD thermal expansion show close agreement with corresponding GPUMD results and published simulation results. A separate 12.5-million-atom Cu shock-compression simulation demonstrates its applicability to large-scale nonequilibrium dynamics. These results support model- and stage-specific specialization as a practical way to accelerate GPU potential evaluation in general-purpose molecular dynamics workflows.

articles.title: FINESSE: A Versatile Beamline for Fundamental Interactions with Neutrons at the European Spallation SourcE
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: FINESSE (A Versatile Beamline for Fundamental Interactions with Neutrons at the European Spallation SourcE) is a proposed versatile beamline for fundamental interactions with neutrons at the European Spallation Source. Building on the HIBEAM design studies, FINESSE extends the original concept into a dual-guide beamline capable of operating either in a high-flux configuration or in a low-background configuration within a single ESS beam port. The high-flux branch is optimized for rare-process searches, including neutron--antineutron oscillations, neutron--sterile-neutron transitions, axion-like-particle searches, neutron charge measurements, and rare neutron decays. The low-background branch is designed for precision measurements requiring strong suppression of prompt and line-of-sight backgrounds, with a cryogenic neutron electric-dipole-moment experiment used as a benchmark case. A baseline exchangeable-guide concept has been developed in which only short guide sections inside the ESS bunker are exchanged, while the upstream extraction system and chopper positions remain fixed. A staged implementation, Short FINESSE, would use the upstream section of the high-flux beamline together with a compact magnetically controlled experimental region, enabling an early physics and R&D programme before completion of the full facility. This paper summarizes the scientific case, beamline concept, guide simulations, chopper and timing system, magnetic-field control, detector developments, and staged implementation strategy. FINESSE would establish a long-term particle-physics infrastructure at ESS, providing a beamline for both discovery-driven searches and precision neutron measurements throughout the lifetime of the facility.
authors: J. Amaral, J. Barrow, M. Bartis, D. H. Beck, P. M. Bentley, J. Bijnens, G. Brooijmans, L. J. Broussard, A. Burgman, G. Cibinetto, G. Croci, D. D. Di Julio, P. Fierlinger, B. W. Filippone, C. Scioscioli, R. Shrock, D. Silvermyr, H. Sina, W. M. Snow, Y. V. Stadnik, L. Tchelidze, N. Tsapatsaris, A. Tureanu, A. Vilela Pereira, M. Wolke, J. Womersley, S. Xu, A. R. Young, K. Osterberg

articles.title: Dynamic Optimization Workflow for Gyrokinetic Stability and Transport
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A dynamic optimization workflow for linear gyrokinetic stability that couples the gyrokinetic code CGYRO with the libEnsemble framework for ensemble management has been developed. The workflow is designed to efficiently explore multi-dimensional plasma parameter spaces and to address the practical challenges of simulation-driven optimization in fusion plasma physics, including expensive objective evaluations, unavailable gradient information, non-smoothness arising from transitions between dominant instability branches, and simultaneous multi-core simulations on high-performance computing resources. Rather than optimizing the growth rate at a single wavenumber, the objective maximizes the growth rate-to-wavenumber ratio over the ion-scale spectrum. A derivative-free, model-based optimization algorithm employs manifold sampling to handle the nonsmooth composite structure of the objective function. The approach is applied to the optimization of local magnetic flux-surface shaping parameters, with an equilibrium baseline drawn from DIII-D negative triangularity experimental parameters. The workflow is general and extensible and provides a foundation for future optimization studies involving nonlinear transport objectives and higher-dimensional parameter spaces.
authors: E. A. Belli, J. Larson, J. Candy, I. Sfiligoi

articles.title: Photoacoustic imaging of human brain function through intact adult skulls
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized noninvasive imaging of human brain function, but it indirectly senses deoxyhemoglobin through water-proton relaxation and relies on bulky, costly, noisy, enclosed, superconducting-magnet scanners. In contrast, photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) directly probes hemoglobin absorption using a more compact, lower-cost, quieter, open, magnet-free system. However, functional PACT of the adult human brain has so far been demonstrated only after surgical skull removal, because the skull strongly attenuates optical and acoustic signals. Here, we demonstrate non-invasive transcranial functional PACT (T-fPACT) through the intact adult skull. A densely packed, high-channel-count (3,072-element) hemispherical ultrasonic array provides near-2π-steradian simultaneous acquisition, enabling high sensitivity and single-shot three-dimensional imaging at 20 Hz that eliminates motion blurring. Participant-specific stabilization further enables measurement of small task-evoked hemodynamic responses over the entire task duration. In healthy adults, T-fPACT localized responses to expected sensorimotor regions, distinguished task-specific motor representations, and yielded consistent localizations across repeated task runs and visits. Comparison with high-field (7 T) fMRI showed spatially corresponding functional regions, while dual-wavelength imaging revealed distinct hemoglobin-weighted responses. These findings overcome the long-standing skull barrier in human brain PACT and establish non-invasive, rapid volumetric photoacoustic imaging of brain function.
authors: Yilin Luo, Rui Cao, Manxiu Cui, Karteekeya Sastry, Kay Jann, Yousuf Aborahama, Geng Ku, Jinhua Xu, Xiaofei Luo, Shuai Na, Samuel Davis, Konstantin Maslov, Yang Zhang, Danny J. Wang, Lihong V. Wang

articles.title: Inverse design of poles and zeros: tailoring phase control in metasurfaces
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a physically interpretable inverse-design framework for generalized Huygens metasurfaces, using prescribed scattering poles and zeros to engineer resonance interference and transmission-phase control. Compared with direct optimization of transmission or reflection coefficients, this approach offers a physically transparent route to rationally controlling resonance properties, including linewidth and group delay, while reducing computational cost. The resulting designs demonstrate how near-unity transmission and 2π phase excursion can arise from resonance interference. These signatures of the Kerker effect extend beyond the conventional alignment of electric and magnetic dipole resonances to other mechanisms, including guided-mode resonances and quasi-bound states in the continuum. We further optimize the Kerker condition across a continuum of refractive-index states in a reconfigurable phase change material metasurface, enabling high-transmission 2π phase tuning. Our results establish a versatile and practical approach to metasurface phase control through the targeted design of scattering poles and zeros.
authors: Junhe Zhang, Seoyoung Kim, Hyun Jung Kim, Juejun Hu

articles.title: Theory of deeply subwavelength electromagnetic structuring of semiconductors due to thermal-ionization instability
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a theory of ionization-assisted instability that governs the reflection of intense electromagnetic pulses from a semiconductor surface. Local overheating of the material increases the free-carrier density and conductivity, which in turn enhances the absorption of the incident radiation and further amplifies local heating and avalanche ionization. At high pump repetition rates, the overheating accumulates from pulse to pulse, leading to a gradual rise of the local material temperature and free carrier density - a positive feedback loop that drives thermal runaway. However, this effect competes with diffraction of the pump field on the emerging perturbation of the dielectric permittivity or on the surface relief, which reduces the local electric field amplitude in the overheated regions, thus providing negative feedback. We show that the competition between heat diffusion and diffraction near-field weakening creates conditions for the exponential growth of temperature perturbations with a certain wavenumber determined by the pulse repetition rate, pump field, thermal conductivity and other material parameters. The derived analytical expressions accurately describe the spatial period of deeply subwavelength structures observed in recent experiments on silicon structuring by intense terahertz radiation, and reproduce qualitatively dependencies of their period on the pump intensity, the incident wavelength and the number of pump pulses.
authors: I. V. Oladyshkin, D. I. Kulshin, E. O. Smolina

articles.title: On-chip optical isolators
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical isolation suppresses back-reflections that destabilize lasers, produce parasitic interference, and increase crosstalk in photonic systems. Although free-space and fibre-optic isolators are mature, no broadly adopted on-chip technology yet combines strong isolation, low insertion loss, broad bandwidth, compact footprint, and scalable fabrication. The difficulty is twofold: Lorentz reciprocity must be broken, and every relevant backward spatial, spectral, and polarization channel must be suppressed. This Review develops a common framework for assessing proposed solutions. We first distinguish pairwise nonreciprocity from intensity-asymmetric transmission and from true isolation using the constitutive relations and scattering matrix. We then compare three physical routes to an integrated nonreciprocal response: magneto-optical bias, externally driven space-time modulation, and nonlinear optical processes. Topological and non-Hermitian systems are treated as cross-cutting design frameworks that can route, protect, or enhance an underlying nonreciprocal response, but do not by themselves break reciprocity. Finally, we examine fundamental constraints and practical trade-offs among isolation, insertion loss, bandwidth, footprint, modal coverage, drive requirements, and fabrication compatibility. The resulting mechanism-based perspective connects reciprocity-breaking physics to the requirements of scalable photonic integrated circuits.
authors: Abanoub Mikhail, Nikolay Solodovchenko, Sen Xu, Fan Zhang, Maksim Tumashov, Mingzhao Song, Sergei Makarov, Andrey Bogdanov

articles.title: A Photonic Integrated Light Generation, Control, and Delivery Engine for Creating Cold Atoms
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The creation of cold atoms underpins quantum sensing and precision metrology, computing, timekeeping, and fundamental science experiments. Miniaturizing the lasers and optical infrastructure, which occupy over 80% of the volume of these experiments, through photonic integration could improve robustness, reliability, and manufacturability while reducing cost and enabling portable space-based precision measurements and quantum tools for non-experts. Yet, there has been limited progress towards integration of the laser and optical infrastructure required to generate cold atoms onto a single chip. We demonstrate a photonic engine that generates, controls, and delivers precision light to create cold atoms in a rubidium 3-dimensional magneto-optical trap (3D-MOT). We integrate on a single chip two frequency-agile self-injection-locked lasers, laser frequency and intensity control, passive beam combining and splitting, signal monitoring, and high-efficiency beam delivery to a rubidium vapor cell. The integrated engine is shown to support multiple functions required for generating cold atoms including stable generation of low-noise cooling and repump light, frequency control for atom spectroscopy and stabilization, real-time laser monitoring, routing for laser offset locking, optical power modulation, and large-area three-beam delivery of 3 mW to the physics package. Fully electrically controlled, the engine enables sustained 3D-MOT operation, trapping more than 1 million atoms at an average temperature of 350 uK and supporting atom-number and temperature measurements. These results demonstrate the first single-chip integration of light generation, control, and delivery for cold-atom generation, offering a path toward smaller, more robust, and manufacturable cold-atom systems for applications including cold-atom clocks and sensors.
authors: Andrei Isichenko, Calisto Ruiz, Chuan Zhong, Nick Montifiore, Sam J. Harding, Meiting Song, Chenghang Liu, Nitin Indukuri, Karl D. Nelson, Daniel J. Blumenthal

articles.title: Validation of geometric proxies using negative and positive triangularity plasmas with varying elongation on TCV and multi-machine gyrokinetic simulations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negative Triangularity (NT) tokamak plasmas can achieve H-mode-like confinement while avoiding Edge Localized Modes, making them an attractive reactor scenario. Predicting in which configuration this benefit occurs requires understanding how magnetic geometry controls turbulent transport. Using a set of geometric proxies based on the poloidally averaged magnetic drift velocity, its poloidal variation, and Finite Larmor Radius (FLR) effects, this work validates their predictive power against gyrokinetic simulations and experiments. First, the proxies are used to predict how the relative benefit of NT over Positive Triangularity (PT) evolves with elongation κ, forecasting a detrimental effect of NT below κsim0.75--0.8. This prediction is confirmed by linear and nonlinear GENE simulations in both ITG- and TEM-dominated regimes. Additionally, a dedicated experimental elongation scan on TCV shows that NT plasmas at κm̊ LCFS=1.5 have β_N and H₉₈y₂ roughly 1.5 times larger than PT counterparts, while no difference is observed at κm̊ LCFS=0.95. The analysis is then extended to realistic ITG-dominated scenarios from DIII-D, AUG, and JET, including up-down asymmetric equilibria where conventional triangularity-based descriptions break down. In all three devices, simulations of NT equilibria exhibit substantially reduced nonlinear heat fluxes relative to PT (factors of 1.8, 1.6, and 2.1, respectively). A systematic swap of geometric coefficients between NT and PT equilibria shows that magnetic drifts and FLR effects are the dominant stabilizing mechanisms across all machines, with parallel dynamics playing a secondary role. These results establish the geometric proxies as reliable, computationally inexpensive predictors of NT transport benefits across diverse shapes and turbulence regimes.
authors: Alessandro Balestri, Justin Ball, Stefano Coda, Olivier Sauter, Paola Mantica, Alberto Mariani, Benoit Labit, Branka Vanovac, Joerg Hobirk, the TCV team

articles.title: All-electron machine-learned orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.17975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce STRUCTURES-P, a machine-learned all-electron orbital-free density functional for periodic CHNO systems. Electrostatics are evaluated analytically in an atom-centered Gaussian basis, while an equivariant network learns the kinetic and exchange-correlation energy from energies and gradients of non-ground-state densities. Minimizing the functional from a superposition of atomic densities recovers the Kohn-Sham ground state: on held-out crystals, the density error falls from 6.7% to 0.4% of the electron count and the energy error reaches 0.25 mHa per atom, half that of a same-architecture interatomic potential. A single functional can be trained for both isolated molecules and periodic systems, and the model generalizes to larger unit cells. It largely preserves relative-energy rankings and reproduces convex-hull vertices on the tested H-N composition slice. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of machine-learned all-electron orbital-free DFT for variational density optimization and energy evaluation in fixed-geometry solids.
authors: Marc K. Ickler, Andreas Hermann, Fred A. Hamprecht

articles.title: Can Machine Learning Potentials Be More Accurate Than the Methods They Are Trained On?
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although machine learning potentials (MLPs) generalize across configurational and chemical compound spaces, their accuracy is commonly believed to be limited by their training methods, with improvements beyond this limit achieved so far only by refitting to experimental observables. In this Perspective, we argue that MLPs can also be made more accurate than their training methods non-empirically by generalizing across a third space, that of quantum-chemical methods. We propose routes to method-transferable MLPs that predict at unseen methods, with working implementations in both density-functional and wavefunction-based theories showing that they can be more accurate than any of their training methods. Aiming beyond the accuracy of the training methods could also make universal MLPs more accurate than single-method models, even when the method-transferable MLPs remain less accurate than those QM methods. Method-transferable MLPs will shape the construction of training datasets and the evaluation of models, pushing the accuracy limits of chemical simulations.
authors: Pavlo O. Dral, Yi-Fan Hou, Yuxinxin Chen, Hassan Nawaz, Mateusz Witkowski, Szymon Śmiga, Ireneusz Grabowski

articles.title: Controlling writhe in stellarator optimization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The writhe of a closed curve measures its coiling, and for a ribbon along it, writhe is the contribution to the linking number not due to twist. In stellarators, large writhe implies large helical excursion and has previously been either an uncontrolled outcome in optimization, or fixed beforehand by the choice of the coordinate system. We present a simple method to target the underlying writhe of the plasma boundary during optimization. Our method calculates writhe and linking number directly from the underlying elliptical boundary of the stellarator. It therefore does not require any properties of the MHD equilibrium solve, such as the true magnetic axis, making it fast to evaluate and smooth to differentiate. Examples for quasi-helically symmetric stellarators show that this target works well in practice.
authors: Tobias M. Schuett, Sophia A. Henneberg

articles.title: Extrapolating Collisional Rate Coefficients for Molecules of Astrophysical Interest Using Neural Networks
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State-to-state rate coefficients for inelastic molecular collisions are essential inputs for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium radiative transfer models, yet their computation using quantum scattering methods is prohibitive for large molecules and highly excited rotational states. We investigate the ability of artificial neural networks to extend existing datasets of collisional excitation rate coefficients without performing additional scattering calculations. A multilayer perceptron model was trained using molecular quantum numbers, level energies, energy gaps, and kinetic temperature as descriptors, and optimized on logarithmic rate coefficients. The model was tested on diverse collision systems ranging from simple diatomic molecules (CO, SiO) to open-shell species (SO), small asymmetric tops (H₂O, SO₂₎, and complex organic molecules (benzonitrile and vinyl cyanide) colliding with H₂ molecules or He atoms. Extrapolations were performed toward higher rotational levels, higher temperatures, and combinations of both. For most systems, predictions of rate coefficients involving previously unseen rotational states yielded mean error factors between 1.1 and 1.5, with the dominant rate coefficients generally reproduced more accurately than weaker transitions. Temperature extrapolations proved particularly successful, while combined extrapolations in temperature and rotational levels remained accurate to within a factor of two in most cases. The prediction quality depends on the interplay between dataset size, temperature range, molecular complexity, and the presence of clear collisional propensity rules. Overall, the approach demonstrates that machine learning can provide a practical route to extending collisional datasets for astrophysical applications, especially for large molecules for which additional quantum-scattering calculations are computationally demanding.

articles.title: Orbital Angular Momentum Transfer and Beam-Quality Limits in Fork-Grating Electron Diffraction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze fork-grating generation of electron vortex beams beyond the ideal single-mode approximation. The incident beam is described as a paraxial Gaussian ensemble with finite transverse momentum spread and a first electromagnetic Hartree phase accumulated before the grating. Within Fresnel propagation we derive an analytical expression for each diffraction order and determine the corresponding orbital-angular-momentum statistics. The mean OAM of a selected order remains fixed by the topological rule, łangle L_zångleₘ₌ₘₚhbar, while its variance is set by the residual transverse momentum spread of the beam prepared at the grating. For the Gaussian mixture, the transverse purity is mathcal Pₚₑᵣₚ,ₘ=[1+2(Δ Lz,ₘ/hbar)²]⁻¹. The observed annular profile is governed by a separate propagation-dependent blurring scale, so a beam can retain well-defined mean OAM while having low transverse purity or a partially filled vortex minimum. Within the radial phase-screen approximation, the Hartree self-field modifies the propagated profile while preserving the full-plane OAM moments and transverse purity.
authors: P. K. Tsiopa, S. S. Baturin

articles.title: The Energetic Particle Detector Instrument on ELFIN
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the design methodology, implementation, and data products of the Energetic Particle Detector (EPD) instrument on-board the Electron Losses and Fields Investigation (ELFIN) dual SmallSat mission. ELFIN was designed to study the time-evolution of energetic particle distributions in Earth's magnetosphere, having operated in polar Low Earth Orbit (LEO) from 2018 to 2022. Each satellite's instrument payload contained a pair of detector heads to sense differential-directional fluxes of 50 keV to sim5 MeV electrons (EPDE), and 50 keV to sim2 MeV atomic ions (EPDI), with an energy resolution better than 50% (Δ E/E<0.5). The satellites were spinning with a nominal period of 2.8 s in a plane containing Earth's background magnetic field, with particle counting intervals subdivided into 16 consecutive spin sectors. Each EPD was paired with a three-axis Fluxgate Magnetometer (FGM) sampled at 80 Hz for local pitch-angle determination. Each detector head operated on the principle of pulse-height analysis (PHA) in solid state media, collimated by a rectangular 22.5ⁱ̧rc field of view and entrance aperture. The EPDE contained a stack of 6 silicon detectors (0.7 cm total thickness) with 0.15 cm² str geometric factor, with ion contamination mitigated by an aperture foil and digital coincidence logic. The EPDI contained a stack of 2 silicon detectors (0.1 cm total thickness) with 0.03 cm² str geometric factor, with electron contamination mitigated by a magnetic broom stage and digital anti-coincidence logic. The total assembled mass, volume, and power required for the EPD detector heads and circuit boards were 939 g, 10×9.8×8.4 cm³, and 2.3 W, respectively. We describe each EPD design element alongside instrument data products and processing.
authors: Colin Wilkins, Ryan Caron, Ethan Tsai, Chris Shaffer, Patrick Cruce, Maxwell Chung, Andrei Runov, Jiang Liu, Drew Turner, Yuri Shprits, Wen Li, Michael Lawson, Emmanuel Masongsong, Cindy Russell, Eric Grimes, Jiashu Wu, Matthew Allen, Jessica Artinger, Alex Flemming, Brayden Hesford, Laura Iglesias, James King, Austin Norris, Carter Pedersen, Daniel Thomlinson, Wynne Turner, Vassilis Angelopoulos

articles.title: Probing topological edge states in multilayer dielectric photonic nanostructures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological photonics has recently attracted a significant attention, leading to many theoretical studies and predictions. However, direct experimental demonstrations of topology-driven effects, particularly in nanostructures, are rarely proven. In this work, we experimentally investigate multilayer photonic nanostructures composed of alternating subwavelength dielectric layers, arranged according to the topological Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By engineering different edge truncations, we probe different supported topological phases. Our theoretical predictions and experimental measurements reveal strong field confinement at the surface exclusively in the configuration supporting topological edge states, providing their localized character and topological origin. First, we demonstrate enhanced absorption in an ultrathin absorbing overlayer deposited on the surface when the topological surface mode is present, highlighting the potential for surface-sensing applications. Second, we observe enhanced second-harmonic generation in reflection from the surface, demonstrating the potential of topological states for surface enhanced nonlinear optics enabled by the strong localization of the electromagnetic field at the interface.
authors: Eva Otero, Ivan Toftul, Michael Scalora, Jose Trull, Crina Cojocaru, Yuri Kivshar

articles.title: Ensuring Complete Consistency between Hops and Wavefunction Propagation in Fewest-Switches Surface Hopping
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.18743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fewest-switches surface hopping (FSSH) is a popular and versatile approach for performing dynamical simulations beyond the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, in which nonadiabatic effects are incorporated through stochastic hops of the active potential energy surface. However, the FSSH algorithm does not ensure that hops are completely consistent with the underlying electronic wavefunction dynamics. This can lead to significant errors as well as requiring small propagation time steps, which can significantly compromise the computational efficiency of the method. These problems are known to be particularly severe at so-called trivial crossings, for which the nonadiabatic coupling is entirely localized at the crossing point. Here, we solve the trivial-crossing problem by developing a fully-consistent hopping-probability formula, which generates attempted hops that match the time-evolution of the wavefunction across any size time step by construction. A state-tracking algorithm is also utilized to ensure that attempted hops are always accepted at trivial crossings. Through application to systems that contain extremely challenging trivial crossings, we demonstrate that this hopping scheme is capable of obtaining highly accurate results, even when large propagation time steps are used.

articles.title: Generalized PINN-Based Inverse Estimation of Spatially Varying Heat Transfer Coefficients with Transfer Learning
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates generalized boundary representations and transfer learning for physics-informed neural-network (PINN) estimation of spatially varying convective heat transfer coefficients (HTCs) in jet impingement cooling. Piecewise-linear (PWL) and neural-network boundary estimators are inferred from transient interior-temperature measurements and evaluated against CFD-CHT reference HTC profiles at Reynolds numbers of 5000, 10000 and 15000. A discrete Adjoint-FEM formulation with gradient regularization based on the H¹⁻seminorm provides an independent inverse-method comparison. Transfer learning is investigated under two source-target conditions: transfer between noise levels at the same Reynolds number, and transfer from a controlled Gaussian-profile problem to CFD-CHT-derived target problems at different Reynolds numbers. For the representative Re = 5000 target with 5% measurement noise, quadratic, PWL, and neural-network PINNs achieve relative HTC-profile errors of 5.08, 5.31 and 5.19%, respectively, while generalized representations reduce the error for the Re = 15000 target from 16.76% for the quadratic PINN to 14.41% and 14.46%. Transfer learning reduces target-training time by 57.86-81.71% for fixed-Reynolds-number transfer and by 50.59-84.94% for Gaussian-to-CHT transfer. Its effect on reconstruction accuracy is target dependent: fixed-profile PWL transfer remains within 0.30 percentage points of scratch training, whereas Gaussian-to-CHT transfer produces differences of 0.10-1.52 percentage points across targets and representations. These results demonstrate that generalized PINN representations can accommodate spatially varying HTC profiles without a prescribed quadratic form, while transfer learning can substantially reduce target-training cost for repeated inverse estimation, with the resulting reconstruction accuracy depending on source-target compatibility.
authors: Pradipan Maitra, Jariful Hassan, Arijit Hazra

articles.title: Physics-Informed State Space Models for Day-Ahead Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting requires both strong temporal modeling and adherence to physical PV system constraints. Purely data-driven models often ignore the underlying PV conversion process and may produce predictions that are outside the operational range of a PV system. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed state space framework that combines a differentiable PV conversion model with a selective state space backbone (PowerMamba). Our approach follows a physics-residual decomposition. The physics module provides a structured baseline based on solar geometry, irradiance, temperature effects, and inverter limits, while the state space model learns residual corrections from numerical weather prediction (NWP) inputs over a 24-hour horizon. Experiments on one year of utility-scale PV data show that the proposed method significantly improves forecasting accuracy, reducing RMSE by 38.5% and MAE by 45.8% compared to a physics-only baseline, and outperforming a purely data-driven model. Results further show that incorporating system-level physics provides the largest performance gains, while additional refinements offer only marginal improvements. Beyond accuracy, the model improves robustness by constraining predictions toward physical feasibility, reducing unrealistic predictions under corrupted measurements.
authors: Phil Aupke, Muhammad Hassan, Khalid Ali, Seema, Andreas Kassler, Andreas Theocharis

articles.title: A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features (R_łambda, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.
authors: Md. Muqtadir Fuad, Md. Istiak Adnan, Ridwan Al Aziz

articles.title: Continuous-Time Cloth Dynamics with Physics-Informed Neural ODEs
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present ContinuousCloth, a continuous-time, physics-informed neural solver for deformable cloth dynamics that enforces a spring--mass ODE within a neural trajectory model. Unlike classical time-stepping simulators that return trajectories only on a discrete integration grid, ContinuousCloth supports querying at arbitrary timestamps and computing displacement, velocity, and acceleration via automatic differentiation. We evaluate ContinuousCloth along two dimensions. In a physics-only setting, ContinuousCloth achieves trajectory accuracy comparable to high-precision solvers across six diverse boundary-condition scenarios while reducing runtime by up to 17.4 times. When fused with sparse and noisy observations, the spring--mass ODE acts as a strong inductive bias for downstream tasks: interpolation and parameter estimation. That is, ContinuousCloth reduces interpolation error by 7.3 times over a data-only neural baseline in simulation and 2.4 times on real-world cloth sequences, and achieves 2.6 times lower parameter error than a differentiable-solver baseline under high-noise conditions, demonstrating consistent robustness under realistic measurement imperfections.
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Zhuo He, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa

articles.title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.14493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows.
